title: gRPC Multiplexed Client Connector Proposal
content:
Context and goal:
This is a personal design scratchpad for a lightweight gRPC client connector that multiplexes many logical sessions/streams over a single physical connection between client-side SDK and a local or edge proxy. Primary goal is to reduce connection churn and memory for mobile/embedded clients while preserving per-session QoS (priority, deadline), per-request tracing, and simple reconnect semantics.

Principles and constraints:
- Keep wire protocol simple (single bidi stream with framed messages).
- Support arbitrary logical sessions (conversation ids) with independent ordering semantics.
- Flow-control: allow both per-connection and per-session backpressure.
- Auth/ACL: reuse existing per-client auth token; still allow session-scoped keys for privileged ops.
- Reconnect: allow stateful resume for hot sessions (KV cache hints, last-ack offsets).
- Low CPU on client; most complexity on proxy/edge service.

High-level message model (informal):
- Every frame carries: envelope { connection_id (implicit), logical_stream_id, seq, type, flags } + payload.
- Types: OPEN_STREAM, CLOSE_STREAM, REQUEST, RESPONSE, ACK, FLOW_UPDATE, HEARTBEAT, SNAPSHOT, MIGRATE.

Sketch proto (very rough, intentionally compact):
// single bidi stream RPC: Connect(multiplex.StreamFrame) returns (stream multiplex.StreamFrame)
message FrameEnvelope {
  string stream_id = 1; // logical id (opaque)
  uint64 seq = 2; // per-stream sequence number for ordering
  FrameType type = 3;
  uint32 flags = 4; // bitfield: priority bits, end-of-message, resumable
  uint32 credits = 5; // optional: used with FLOW_UPDATE
}
message StreamFrame {
  FrameEnvelope env = 1;
  bytes payload = 2; // application payload (e.g., HTTP/1.1 like request bytes, or serialized JSON)
  // optional meta headers as serialized kv pairs to avoid repeated round trips
  repeated KeyValue meta = 3;
}
enum FrameType {
  OPEN = 0;
  REQUEST = 1;
  RESPONSE = 2;
  ACK = 3;
  FLOW_UPDATE = 4;
  HEARTBEAT = 5;
  CLOSE = 6;
  SNAPSHOT = 7;
  MIGRATE = 8;
}
message KeyValue { string k = 1; string v = 2; }

Notes on ordering and semantics:
- Each logical stream maintains a simple seq counter. Clients increment on each REQUEST; server echoes ACKs with seq to confirm.
- Responses may arrive out-of-order at the connection level but must be ordered per-stream (server-side must buffer to preserve per-stream ordering unless flags allow unordered responses for streaming ops).
- For low-latency ops, clients can set flags to indicate idempotent/unordered requests.

Flow control: credits and windowing
- Two levels: connection-level credit (how many frames client can send before waiting) and per-stream credit.
- FLOW_UPDATE frames carry additional credits.
- Policy: default connection window 64 frames, per-stream window 8; proxy can uplift per-stream windows dynamically (for high-throughput streams).

Priority lanes and QoS
- Flags include 3-bit priority (0..7). Proxy scheduler should attempt to drain higher priority streams first, but not completely starve lower priority ones.
- Implement a token-bucket scheme per-priority lane.

Auth and tenant isolation
- Primary auth is at connection establishment (existing OIDC/JWT token).
- Streams can include an optional session_token meta header if a sub-scope is required; proxy will validate and map to session ACLs.
- Audit logs: each frame includes sampling bits for tracing; full traces can be rehydrated at proxy using stream_id + seq mapping.

Reconnect and resume
- On connection loss client should open a new physical connection and send OPEN frames for streams to resume; send MIGRATE frame indicating previous connection_id and last_seq per-stream.
- Proxy maintains ephemeral session entries for a short TTL (e.g., 60s) to allow resume; longer-term state should be persisted by the upstream service (or client periodically snapshot).
- SNAPSHOT frames allow client to push small state hints (KV checksums, last-response-hash) to help server fast-path resume.

Session migration (moving streams between proxies)
- Useful when client moves to a different network/regional proxy.
- MIGRATE frame semantics: client requests migration, carries proof-of-ownership (connection-level token), optional snapshot. Proxy coordinates with target proxy (out-of-band control plane) and responds with ACK when streams are safe to continue.

Example YAML connector config (client SDK):
connector:
  conn_retry:
    max_attempts: 6
    base_backoff_ms: 250
  windows:
    connection_frames: 128
    default_stream_frames: 16
  priority:
    lanes: 4
    default: 2
  resume:
    enabled: true
    ttl_seconds: 60
  heartbeat_interval_ms: 15000

ASCII diagram (connection-level):
Client SDK <--(single bidi gRPC stream)---> LocalProxy/Edge ---> Redwood Inference frontends
|-- multiple logical stream_ids (conv A, conv B, embed-req-1, rerank-3) over same underlying TCP/TLS/gRPC channel --|

Example handshake flow (sequence):
1) Client: Connect() stream established; sends OPEN (client metadata + auth)
2) Proxy: returns OPEN_ACK with assigned connection_id, initial credits
3) Client: issues OPEN for logical stream s1 (user conversation), sets priority=3
4) Server: ACCEPTs stream request; future frames on s1 will be REQUEST/RESPONSE pairs
5) During heavy load proxy sends FLOW_UPDATE to reduce client send rate

Edge cases and notes:
- Long-poll vs streaming: allow a flag on stream OPEN to select semantics; streaming uses streaming responses and can be incremental (partial responses) with intermediate seqs.
- Binary payloads: payload must be opaque bytes; higher layers decide marshaling (protobuf, JSON, raw text).
- Max frame size: 1MB default, configurable; large payloads should be chunked and reassembled per-stream.
- Client offline batching: client SDK can queue requests when offline and replay with original timestamps; must be mindful of replay semantics for non-idempotent ops.

Observability:
- Include sample bits in meta header to indicate full-trace collection. Proxy logs must map stream_id->trace_id.
- Per-stream metrics exported: requests/sec, avg-latency, error-rate, outstanding_credits.

Open questions / TODOs (action items):
- Q: Should we reuse existing HTTP/2 stream semantics (i.e., map gRPC underlying streams) or keep our simpler envelope?
  - tradeoff: HTTP/2 streams give native prioritization and flow-control but are harder to multiplex across transports and to implement consistently on mobile.
- Q: Should we push ordering responsibility to client or server? Current draft puts seq and ordering responsibilities mostly on server with client providing seq for safety.
- Q: How to handle mid-stream auth changes (user logs out/logs in)? Propose special REAUTH frame.
- Implement small PoC: client-side node-js shim + Go proxy that speaks envelope proto. Spike priority scheduling and backpressure behavior.

Quick spike plan (2-week):
- Week 1: proto and minimal Go server that accepts frames, enforces per-stream windows, and echoes. Create node client shim that opens multiple logical streams and runs basic scenarios (N concurrent convs, high priority vs low).
- Week 2: add reconnect/resume, snapshot handling, and simple priority scheduler. Collect perf numbers: connection memory per-conv, latency tail under contention.

Bench hypotheses:
- One physical gRPC connection with muxing should reduce socket churn by ~10x and memory per-conversation by ~40% for mobile clients that maintain many idle convs.
- Tail latency improves for high-priority lanes if token-bucket per-lane is implemented.

Notes to self: keep this doc intentionally informal; share with Marco and Li before wider distribution. Record results of spike in follow-up doc and extract minimal proto into GH.

References and inspirations:
- HTTP/2 multiplexing and priorities (observe pitfalls)
- QUIC stream framing and migration semantics (good migration model)
- Existing grpc-multiplexer libs (search later)

End of scratchpad.
